content: Typhoid fever and paratyphoid fever are diseases caused by specific types of bacteria. Typhoid fever is caused by Salmonella Typhi, while paratyphoid fever is caused by Salmonella Paratyphi. These bacteria can be transmitted from an infected person to others, primarily through poor hygiene practices. For example, if an infected individual uses the bathroom and does not wash their hands properly, the bacteria can remain on their hands and contaminate surfaces, food, or drinks that they touch. In regions with inadequate sanitation, water used for rinsing or preparing food and beverages, including tap water, can also become contaminated with these bacteria. Travelers who consume contaminated food or drinks are at risk of becoming ill. Both typhoid fever and paratyphoid fever present with similar symptoms. Affected individuals typically experience a high fever, which can reach 103–104°F (39–40°C). Other symptoms may include weakness, abdominal pain, headache, diarrhea or constipation, cough, and loss of appetite. Some patients may develop a rash characterized by flat, rose-colored spots. Although rare, complications such as internal bleeding and death can occur. Typhoid and paratyphoid fever are most prevalent in areas of the world where water and food safety are compromised, and sanitation is poor. Travelers to regions such as Eastern and Southern Asia (notably Pakistan, India, and Bangladesh), Africa, the Caribbean, Central and South America, and the Middle East are at an increased risk of contracting these diseases. Individuals visiting friends or relatives in these regions are particularly vulnerable, as they may stay longer, consume local home-prepared food, and may not take precautions such as vaccination before traveling. In the United States, approximately 425 cases of typhoid fever and 125 cases of paratyphoid fever are diagnosed annually, with most cases linked to international travel. To prevent typhoid fever, travelers should consider vaccination, practice careful selection of food and beverages, and maintain proper hand hygiene. It is recommended to check whether typhoid vaccination is advised for your travel destination. Two types of typhoid vaccines are available in the United States: 1. Oral vaccine (pill form): This vaccine is suitable for individuals aged 6 years and older. It requires taking four pills (one every other day), and the full course should be completed at least one week before travel. 2. Injectable vaccine (shot form): This vaccine is suitable for individuals aged 2 years and older. A single shot (or booster shot) should be administered at least two weeks before travel. It is important to note that typhoid vaccines are only 50–80% effective, so travelers should still exercise caution regarding what they eat and drink to minimize their risk of infection. Additionally, there is no vaccine available to protect against paratyphoid fever. For these reasons, it is crucial to adopt additional preventive measures, such as avoiding potentially contaminated food and water, even if vaccinated.
